'''Moustafa T. Chahine''' (1 January 1935 - 23 March 2011) was an atmospheric scientist and an international leader in atmospheric [[remote sensing]] using satellite observations.<ref name=parkinson>{{cite book |last=Parkinson |first=Claire |title=Moustafa Chahine |year=2012 |url=https://www.nap.edu/read/13338/chapter/10#47 |publisher=National Academies Press|doi=10.17226/13338 |isbn=978-0-309-25280-5 }}</ref> He was the Science Team Leader for the [[Atmospheric Infrared Sounder]] on [[NASA]]'s [[Earth Observing System]] [[Aqua (satellite)|Aqua]] satellite, and the Chairman of the [[Global Energy and Water Exchanges]] (GEWEX) Science Steering Group of the [[World Climate Research Program]] (WCRP).

== Education ==
Chahine was born in [[Beirut]], Lebanon. He moved to the U.S. in 1954 and attended the [[University of Washington]], receiving the [[B.S.]] and [[M.S.]] degrees in aeronautical engineering in 1956 and 1957, respectively. He received the [[Ph.D.]] in mechanical engineering from the [[University of California at Berkeley]] in 1960, before moving to start his career at the [[Jet Propulsion Laboratory]] ([[JPL]]) of the [[California Institute of Technology]].

== Career ==
At [[JPL]], Chahine initially studied [[shock wave]]s generated by space capsules reentering the Earth atmosphere. He then worked on methods to derive atmospheric temperature and composition information from radiation received remotely from instruments in space. He developed a [[relaxation method]] for exact inverse solution of the [[radiative transfer equation]], and applied it successfully to derive Earth atmospheric temperature and water vapor profiles. He also used the method to derive atmospheric temperature and composition profiles for the atmospheres of [[Venus]], [[Mars]] and [[Jupiter]]. Chahine and colleagues extended his method to include complementary information from Earth-orbiting [[atmospheric sounding|infrared and microwave sounder instruments]], accounting for the presence of clouds, to produce the first maps of [[global surface temperature]] from space.<ref name=parkinson/>

Chahine was the Science Team Leader for the [[Atmospheric Infrared Sounder]] (AIRS), an instrument designed to measure atmospheric and surface temperature, [[water vapor]] and cloud properties, as well as trace [[greenhouse gases]] such as [[ozone]], [[carbon monoxide]], [[carbon dioxide]], and [[methane]], which he successfully proposed for development starting in 1978. He became a member of the Earth System Science Committee (ESSC) of the [[National Academy of Sciences]], chaired by [[Francis Bretherton]], which formulated the science rationale for a NASA multidecadal [[Earth Observing System]] (EOS).<ref>{{cite book |last=National Research Council |date=1988 |title=Earth System Science: A Closer View | publisher=National Academies Press}}</ref> The AIRS instrument was formally selected as part of the [[Earth Observing System]] (EOS) in 1988, and was launched on the second EOS platform, the Aqua satellite, in 2002.

A major advance using AIRS data was Chahine's derivation of atmospheric [[carbon dioxide]] ({{CO2|link=yes}}) in the mid-troposphere. Chahine produced the first satellite-derived global map of atmospheric {{CO2}}, while animations of several years of data displayed the global distributions of both the seasonal cycle and the long-term upward trend in atmospheric {{CO2}}.<ref>{{cite web |last=Castelvecchi |first=Davide |date=17 December 2009 |title=With One Space Observatory Down, NASA Uses Another to Map {{CO2}} |url= https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/space-observatory-co2-nasa/ |publisher=Scientific American}}</ref>

The science data products from AIRS were widely praised.<ref name=parkinson/> In 2006, a study by scientists at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration demonstrated that use of AIRS data in weather forecasting models significantly improved forecast "skill".<ref>{{cite web |date=7 May 2012 |title=NASA weather 'eye in the sky' marks 10 years |url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2012/05/120507092743.htm |publisher=ScienceDaily}}</ref> The current generation of European meteorological satellites now host an AIRS-like sounder, the [[Infrared Atmospheric Sounding Interferometer]]; while a similar instrument, the [[Suomi NPP|Cross-track Infrared Sounder]], was launched in 2011 aboard [[NASA]]'s new [[Suomi NPP]] satellite, the forerunner of the next-generation of U.S. weather satellites.

In 1989 Chahine became the first chairman of the Science Steering Group of the [[World Climate Research Program]]'s [[Global Energy and Water Exchanges|Global Energy and Water Cycle Experiment]] (GEWEX). He served in this role until 1999, during which time the steering group established important connections amongst the international GEWEX community, bringing together satellite-based data collection and climate modeling.<ref>{{cite web |title=New Chairman of GEWEX Scientific Steering Group (SSG) |url= http://www.gewex.org/gewex-content/files_mf/1431982637May1999.pdf |publisher=GEWEX}}</ref>

== Honors ==
* Member of U.S. National Academy of Engineering<ref>{{cite web|last=O’Keefe|first=Mary|date=19 February 2009|title=Local says he's surprised by high honor|url=https://www.latimes.com/socal/la-canada-valley-sun/news/tn-vsl-xpm-2009-02-19-lnws-chahine-story.html|work=Los Angeles Times}}</ref>
* NASA Exceptional Scientific Achievement Medal, 1969 
* [[NASA Outstanding Leadership Medal]], 1984 
* William T. Pecora Award, 1989<ref>{{cite web |title=William T. Pecora Award |url= https://prd-wret.s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/assets/palladium/production/s3fs-public/atoms/files/1989Pecora_Signed_Chahine.pdf}}</ref> 
* AMS Jule G. Charney Award, 1991 
* AIAA Losey Atmospheric Sciences Award, 1993 
* COSPAR William Nordberg Medal, 2002 
* NASA Exceptional Scientific Achievement, 2007 
* SPIE George W. Goddard Award, 2010.<ref>{{cite web |date=25 February 2010 |title=Moustafa Chahine honored with George W. Goddard Award |url= https://spie.org/about-spie/spie-member-news/goddard-2-25-10?SSO=1 |publisher=SPIE}}</ref>
